Information since September points to a still-strong labor market and moderate growth, but softness in business fixed investment and exports. Because investment depends on interest rates and internal funds—and inventory/fixed investment are sensitive to financing conditions—the rate cut to 1.50–1.75% and the Desk’s T-bill purchases and repo operations should ease credit frictions and support capex (Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein, 1994). With overall and core inflation below 2% and market-based inflation compensation low, New Keynesian evidence that expectations feed into realized inflation (Galí and Gertler, 1999; Woodford, 2003) supports accommodation to keep inflation expectations anchored to the symmetric 2% goal. The ample-reserves operating framework helps maintain control over short-term rates and mitigates money market pressures, reinforcing policy transmission via the interest-rate channel while limiting adverse liquidity effects (Woodford, 2003; McCallum and Nelson, 1999). Persistent weakness in external demand is consistent with open-economy models where global shocks depress output and inflation (Obstfeld–Rogoff). Overall, the stance is modestly positive for the outlook—supporting sustained expansion with limited inflation risk—yet tempered by investment and trade headwinds and uncertainty (Romer and Romer; Sims).
